thesis: A system is team-owned when anyone on the rotation can understand, operate and change it: clear ownership boundaries, documented runbooks and design records, shared on-call, boring technology, and no component that only one person can fix. Hero dependence is a design flaw, not a staffing detail.
pitch: I'd start with ownership: every service, job and data store has one owning team, recorded in a catalogue used for alerts and reviews, with boundaries matching team boundaries so a team can change its system without coordinating with five others. Then make knowledge transferable: runbooks for every alert, design docs and decision records for the why, and onboarding that includes doing real operational tasks. On-call is shared by the whole team on a sustainable rotation, which spreads knowledge and makes pain visible to everyone, motivating fixes. Technology choices favour things many people already know. And I'd actively look for heroes: if one person is always pulled into incidents for a component, that's a risk to fix with pairing, documentation and simplification, not a person to praise and rely on. Measure it: can someone new to the team handle a typical incident with the runbook alone?

points.d: Every component owned by one team in a service catalogue, linked to alerts, dashboards and docs.
Systems divided so each team can change and deploy its part independently, reducing coordination and diffusion of responsibility.
Operational knowledge and design reasoning written down where the team can find them.
The whole team rotates, sustainably. Knowledge spreads, and the people who build the system feel its operational pain.
Fewer specialised components means fewer specialists required.
Track who gets pulled into incidents; pair, document and simplify until others can handle those components.
Game days and onboarding tasks where newer team members handle realistic incidents using only docs and tools.

decision: Make ownership, documentation and shared on-call explicit requirements for production readiness. Treat a bus factor of one on a critical component as a risk with an owner and a deadline.
numbers: On-call sustainability guide: rotations of at least several people (Google's SRE book suggests a minimum of around eight for a single-site 24/7 rotation) so on-call doesn't burn people out.
pitfalls: Components 'owned' by everyone, meaning no one.
Rewarding heroics in incidents instead of fixing what made heroics necessary.
On-call only for a few senior engineers.
Documentation written once at launch and never updated.

followups.q: A key engineer is the only one who understands the billing engine. What do you do?
followups.a: Schedule pairing and shadowing, have others lead the next changes and incidents with their support, write runbooks from their knowledge, and simplify the scariest parts.

followups.q: How do you assign ownership for shared libraries or platforms?
followups.a: A platform team owns them as products, with clear support channels and versioning; consuming teams own their use of them.

followups.q: How do you know ownership is working?
followups.a: Incidents are resolved by whoever is on call, without escalation to specific individuals, and changes ship without cross-team coordination.

example: Incident data showed one engineer joined 70% of payment incidents. Over a quarter, the team wrote runbooks from their knowledge, paired on every payment change, and had others lead game days. The next two payment incidents were resolved by on-call engineers alone.
